title: Parenting: decision-making, parenting time and contact
intro: This guide explains, in general terms, what Ontario’s Children’s Law Reform Act and the federal Divorce Act say about decision-making responsibility, parenting time, contact and the best interests of the child. It describes what the law says; it does not say how a court would decide any particular family’s situation.

sections.heading: Words the law uses
paragraphs: In Ontario’s Children’s Law Reform Act, “decision-making responsibility” means “responsibility for making significant decisions about a child’s well-being, including with respect to,” health, education, culture, language, religion and spirituality, and significant extra-curricular activities. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))

“Parenting time” means “the time a child spends in the care of a parent of the child, whether or not the child is physically with the parent during that time”. “Contact” means “the time a child spends in the care of a person other than the child’s parent, whether or not the child is physically with the person during that time”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))

The Act says that, unless the context requires otherwise, “a reference in an Act or regulation to custody of a child, including lawful custody or legal custody of a child, includes reference to decision-making responsibility with respect to the child under this Act”. A reference to access to a child includes parenting time or contact. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (5), (6))

The federal Divorce Act uses the same ideas. It defines decision-making responsibility as “the responsibility for making significant decisions about a child’s well-being”, including health, education, culture, language, religion and spirituality, and significant extra-curricular activities. Parenting time is “the time that a child of the marriage spends in the care of a person referred to in subsection 16.1(1), whether or not the child is physically with that person during that entire time”. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))

sections.heading: Which Act, and who can apply
paragraphs: The Divorce Act deals with a “child of the marriage”. That means “a child of two spouses or former spouses who, at the material time,” is under the age of majority and has not withdrawn from their charge, or is the age of majority or over and under their charge but unable, by reason of illness, disability or other cause, to withdraw from their charge or to obtain the necessaries of life. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))

For Ontario, “court” in the Divorce Act means “the Superior Court of Justice”. The definition also includes any other court in the province whose judges are appointed by the Governor General and that the province designates as a court for the purposes of the Act. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))

Under the Divorce Act, a court may make a parenting order on application by “either or both spouses” or by “a person, other than a spouse, who is a parent of the child, stands in the place of a parent or intends to stand in the place of a parent.” A person in that second group may apply “only with leave of the court.” (Divorce Act, s. 16.1 (1), (3))

Under the Children’s Law Reform Act, “A parent of a child may apply to a court for a parenting order respecting,” decision-making responsibility and parenting time. Any person other than a parent, “including a grandparent,” may apply for a parenting order about decision-making responsibility, or for a contact order. In this Act, “court” means “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court or the Superior Court of Justice”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, ss. 18 (1), 21 (1)-(3))

If a divorce action is started under the Divorce Act, an application under this Part of the Children’s Law Reform Act about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact that has not been determined “is stayed except by leave of the court.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 27)

A person applying under the Children’s Law Reform Act for a parenting order or contact order files an affidavit with “the person’s proposed plan for the child’s care and upbringing”, information about their involvement in any family proceedings or criminal proceedings, and other information relevant to the best-interests factors in section 24. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 21 (4))

Neither Act, in the text this site holds, contains one general statement that sorts parents into one Act or the other by whether they were married. This site does not yet have a source for such a rule. (Children’s Law Reform Act, ss. 21, 27; Divorce Act, ss. 2 (1), 16.1)

sections.heading: The best interests of the child
paragraphs: In making a parenting order or contact order, the court “shall only take into account the best interests of the child in accordance with this section.” The court considers all factors related to the child’s circumstances and gives “primary consideration to the child’s physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (1), (2))

The listed factors include the child’s needs, given age and stage of development, “such as the child’s need for stability”; the nature and strength of the child’s relationship with each parent, siblings, grandparents and other important people; “each parent’s willingness to support the development and maintenance of the child’s relationship with the other parent”; the history of care of the child; and “the child’s views and preferences, giving due weight to the child’s age and maturity, unless they cannot be ascertained”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (3))

Other listed factors are the child’s cultural, linguistic, religious and spiritual upbringing and heritage, “including Indigenous upbringing and heritage”; any plans for the child’s care; each person’s ability and willingness to care for and meet the child’s needs, and to communicate and co-operate; any family violence and its impact; and “any civil or criminal proceeding, order, condition or measure that is relevant to the safety, security and well-being of the child.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (3))

The court “shall not take into consideration the past conduct of any person, unless the conduct is relevant to the exercise of the person’s decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with respect to the child.” In allocating parenting time, the court applies the principle that “a child should have as much time with each parent as is consistent with the best interests of the child.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (5), (6))

The Divorce Act has the same structure. “The court shall take into consideration only the best interests of the child of the marriage in making a parenting order or a contact order.” It lists factors in nearly the same words, speaking of each “spouse” where the Ontario Act speaks of each “parent”, and it applies the principle that “a child should have as much time with each spouse as is consistent with the best interests of the child.” (Divorce Act, s. 16 (1), (3), (6))

sections.heading: Family violence
paragraphs: The Children’s Law Reform Act defines family violence as “any conduct by a family member towards another family member that is violent or threatening, that constitutes a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour, or that causes the other family member to fear for their own safety or for that of another person, and, in the case of a child, includes direct or indirect exposure to such conduct”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))

The conduct “need not constitute a criminal offence”. It includes physical abuse (including forced confinement, but not reasonable force to protect oneself or another person), sexual abuse, threats to kill or cause bodily harm, harassment including stalking, failure to provide the necessaries of life, psychological abuse, financial abuse, threats to kill or harm an animal or damage property, and killing or harming an animal or damaging property. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (2))

When considering the impact of family violence, the court takes into account “the nature, seriousness and frequency of the family violence and when it occurred”; “whether there is a pattern of coercive and controlling behaviour in relation to a family member”; whether the violence is directed toward the child or the child is directly or indirectly exposed to it; and “the physical, emotional and psychological harm or risk of harm to the child”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (4))

The court also takes into account any compromise to the safety of the child or other family member; whether the violence causes the child or other family member to fear for their own safety or that of another person; any steps taken by the person engaging in the violence “to prevent further family violence from occurring and improve the person’s ability to care for and meet the needs of the child”; and “any other relevant factor.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 24 (4))

The Divorce Act defines family violence in similar words, covering conduct “whether or not the conduct constitutes a criminal offence”, and lists the same kinds of conduct. It sets out the same factors for the court to consider about the impact of family violence. (Divorce Act, ss. 2 (1), 16 (4))

sections.heading: What a parenting or contact order can say
paragraphs: On an application under section 21, the court may grant decision-making responsibility to one or more persons, parenting time to one or more parents of the child, or contact to one or more persons other than a parent, according to the kind of application made under that section. It may “determine any aspect of the incidents of the right to decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact”. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (1) (a), (b))

The court may also make “any additional order the court considers necessary and proper in the circumstances”. The listed examples include orders limiting contact or communication between any of the parties, or between a party and the child, and prohibiting a party or other person from engaging in specified conduct in the child’s presence or at any time when the person is responsible for the child’s care. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (1) (c))

Other listed examples are orders prohibiting a party from changing the child’s residence, school or day care facility, or removing the child from Ontario, without another party’s consent or a court order; requiring delivery of the child’s passport, health card or another specified document; requiring a party to give, or consent to the release of, information about the child’s well-being; and requiring a party to facilitate the child’s communication with another party or person. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (1) (c))

The court may allocate decision-making responsibility, “or any aspect of it, to one or more persons”, and may allocate parenting time “by way of a schedule.” Unless the court orders otherwise, a person with parenting time “has exclusive authority during that time to make day-to-day decisions affecting the child.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (4)-(6))

The court includes in a parenting order or contact order any written parenting plan the parties submit with the elements they agree on, “subject to any changes the court may specify if it considers it to be in the best interests of the child to do so.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (7))

Unless a court orders otherwise, a person granted decision-making responsibility or parenting time under a parenting order may ask for and, “subject to any applicable laws”, receive information about the child’s well-being, including health and education. The information may come from any other person granted decision-making responsibility or parenting time under a parenting order, or from any other person likely to have it. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 28 (8))

The Divorce Act gives similar powers. An order may allocate parenting time and decision-making responsibility, may “require that parenting time or the transfer of the child from one person to another be supervised”, and may “authorize or prohibit the relocation of the child.” A contact order can be made on application by “a person other than a spouse”, with leave of the court unless leave was already obtained under section 16.1. (Divorce Act, ss. 16.1 (4), (7), (8), 16.5 (1), (3))

In deciding on a contact order under the Divorce Act, the court considers all relevant factors, “including whether contact between the applicant and the child could otherwise occur, for example during the parenting time of another person.” (Divorce Act, s. 16.5 (4))

The Divorce Act also sets out duties. A person with parenting time, decision-making responsibility or contact “shall exercise that time, responsibility or contact in a manner that is consistent with the best interests of the child.” A party “shall, to the best of their ability, protect any child of the marriage from conflict arising from the proceeding.” (Divorce Act, ss. 7.1, 7.2)

sections.heading: Changing an existing order
paragraphs: Under the Children’s Law Reform Act, a court shall not vary a parenting order or contact order “unless there has been a material change in circumstances that affects or is likely to affect the best interests of the child who is the subject of the order.” A relocation in accordance with section 39.4 is a material change in circumstances. If a court had prohibited the relocation, it “does not, in itself, constitute a material change in circumstances.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 29 (1), (2))

Under the Divorce Act, before varying a parenting order or contact order, the court shall “satisfy itself that there has been a change in the circumstances of the child since the making of the order or the last variation order made in respect of the order”. The relocation of a child is deemed to be a change in circumstances, but a relocation a court has prohibited is not, in itself, such a change. (Divorce Act, s. 17 (5), (5.2), (5.3))

sections.heading: Moving: notice rules under the Children’s Law Reform Act
paragraphs: The Act defines “relocation” as a change in residence of the child, or of a person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time (or an applicant for a parenting order), that “is likely to have a significant impact on the child’s relationship with” another such person or a person who has contact under a contact order. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))

For a change in residence that is not a relocation, a person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time notifies the other people with decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact. The notice is in writing and sets out the expected date of the change and the new address and contact information. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.1 (1), (2), (5))

For a relocation, the notice is given “at least 60 days before the expected date of the proposed relocation”. It is in the form prescribed by the regulations or, if no form is prescribed, in writing. It sets out the expected date, the new address and contact information, “a proposal as to how decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact, as the case may be, could be exercised”, and any other information the regulations prescribe. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.3 (1), (2))

On application, the court may provide that the notice rules do not apply, or apply with changes it specifies, if it is of the opinion that it is appropriate to do so, “including if there is a risk of family violence.” That application “may be made without notice to any other party.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, ss. 39.1 (3), (4), 39.2 (4), (5), 39.3 (3), (4))

A person with decision-making responsibility or parenting time who receives a relocation notice may, “no later than 30 days after receiving the notice,” object by notifying the person who gave it, in writing with reasons and their views on the proposal, or by making an application under section 21. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.3 (5), (6))

A person who has given notice of a proposed relocation in accordance with section 39.3 may relocate the child as of the date in the notice if the relocation is authorized by a court, or if no objection is made in accordance with subsection 39.3 (5) “and there is no order prohibiting the relocation.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (2))

In deciding whether to authorize a relocation, the court considers the best interests of the child under section 24, and also the reasons for the relocation, its impact on the child, and the time spent with the child, and involvement in the child’s life, of each person with parenting time or a pending parenting application. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (3) (a)-(c))

The court also considers compliance with notice requirements and any applicable order, award or agreement; any order, award or agreement specifying where the child is to reside; the reasonableness of the proposal, including travel expenses; and each person’s compliance with their obligations and likelihood of future compliance. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (3) (d)-(g))

The court “shall not consider whether, if the child’s relocation were to be prohibited, the person who intends to relocate the child would relocate without the child or not relocate.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (4))

If the parties substantially comply with an order, family arbitration award or agreement providing that the child spend “substantially equal time in the care of each party”, the party who intends to relocate the child must prove the relocation would be in the child’s best interests. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (5))

If they substantially comply with one providing that the child spend “the vast majority of time” in the care of the party who intends to relocate, the opposing party must prove the relocation would not be in the child’s best interests. In any other case, both parties have the burden of proving whether it is. (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (6), (7))
If the order behind either of the first two burden rules is an interim order, “the court may determine that the subsection does not apply.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.4 (8))

A person who has contact under a contact order and intends to change residence also gives written notice. If the change is likely to have a significant impact on the child’s relationship with that person, the notice is given “at least 60 days before the date on which the change is expected to occur.” (Children’s Law Reform Act, s. 39.2 (1)-(3))

sections.heading: Moving: notice rules under the Divorce Act
paragraphs: The Divorce Act has parallel rules. For a change of residence that is not a relocation, written notice sets out the expected date and the new address and contact information. For a relocation, notice is given “at least 60 days before the expected date of the proposed relocation and in the form prescribed by the regulations”. (Divorce Act, ss. 16.7, 16.8 (1), (2), 16.9 (1), (2))

The court may, on application, provide that the notice requirements do not apply or modify them, “including where there is a risk of family violence.” The application may be made without notice to any other party. (Divorce Act, ss. 16.8 (3), (4), 16.9 (3), (4))

A person with parenting time or decision-making responsibility who has received a relocation notice may object “within 30 days after the day on which the notice is received”, in a prescribed form or in an application under subsection 16.1(1) or paragraph 17(1)(b). The person who gave notice under section 16.9 may relocate the child as of the date in the notice if a court authorizes it, or if there is no such objection and no order prohibiting the relocation. (Divorce Act, s. 16.91 (1))

In deciding whether to authorize a relocation, the court considers, “in addition to the factors referred to in section 16,” a list of factors in close to the same words as the Ontario Act. The burden-of-proof rules are also parallel, and a court “may decide not to apply” the first two of them if the order involved is an interim order. (Divorce Act, ss. 16.92, 16.93, 16.94)
